newsitem.title: USA: U.S. moves to keep peace process alive.
newsitem.headline: U.S. moves to keep peace process alive.

text.p: Seeking to keep the Mideast peace process alive, the United States on Monday rescheduled a Washington visit for Jordan's King Hussein and pressured Yasser Arafat to crack down on Palestinian militants.
A trip to the region by U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross was under consideration but far from being set, officials said.

The White House said Hussein would meet President Bill Clinton in Washington on April 1 and denied the peace process was unravelling. A senior Palestinian official, Yasser Abed Rabbo, met on Monday with Israeli President Ezer Weizman on the crisis, a senior U.S. official said.

Still, as part of a campaign to shore up the embattled peace process, Ross, in a television interview, underscored the need "for 100 percent effort" in fighting terrorism and said "we'd like to see them (Palestinians) do more."

At a briefing, State Department spokesman John Dinger put out a similar message: "What we believe is important now is for Chairman Arafat and the Palestinian Authority to demonstrate through words and deeds that there is definitely no green light" in support of extremist acts.
Senior officials said they expect Arafat, the Palestinan president, to re-arrest guerrilla operatives he freed who are believed responsible for terror bombings against Israel.

"I don't think he (Arafat) has any choice. This is the most delicate time on most delicate issues. (It's) more important now perhaps than ever that we build the right climate" between Israel and Palestinians, one official said.
Officials said Ross was mulling a Middle East trip after last Friday's suicide bombing in Tel Aviv, which put serious new strain on peace talks between Israel and Palestinians.

But they stressed that, contrary to rumours in the region, no decision had been made and that Ross, for the moment, was focused on trying to get Israel and the Palestinian Authority back into a meaningful dialogue.

Washington is not pleased Arafat left for South Asia last Saturday, making it impossible to hold serious talks between the two sides. One official: "We won't be able to stabilise the situation until we have them back talking with each other."

Hussein was set to meet Clinton on March 18, but his visit was postponed after a Jordanian soldier shot dead seven Israeli girls near the Israel-Jordan border on March 13 and after Clinton had knee surgery on March 14.

In addition to the killing of the Israeli girls, an Islamist suicide bomber killed three Israeli women at a Tel Aviv cafe on Friday, further harming Israel-PLO ties already strained over a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

In an effort to breathe new life into the peace process, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak have all met Clinton in Washington over the past six weeks.

Asked if the peace process was now unravelling, White House spokesman Mike McCurry replied: "No ... Manifestly the majority of Arabs and Jews want to see peace in that region. They have seen the benefits and the dividend of peace and they want leaders, and they want those who help the parties, to continue to make progress."
"They don't want to see the cycle descend to violence and terror, which are the weapons of those who are enemies of peace," he said.

Ross, on the MSNBC cable television network, said: "At this point our focus is on intensive contact with the parties, trying to focus on how we can best stabilise the situation ... create a new sense of security on both sides (and) ... an environment where it's possible to move forward again."
U.S. officials said for some time they had been concerned Arafat had softened a crackdown that left two Islamic extremist groups, Hamas and Islamic Jihad, nearly broken.
